title: TCP Connections
summary:
A TCP connection is **not a pipe**. Nothing in the network is dedicated to it. Routers forward independent packets, which may take different paths, arrive out of order or get lost. The "connection" is **shared state kept by the two endpoints' kernels**: sequence numbers, a record of what has been acknowledged, retransmission timers, and a flow-control window. That state is what lets two applications see a reliable, ordered byte stream on top of an unreliable network.

In Linux terms: **TCP socket = 4-tuple + send/receive queues + state machine**. The 4-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port) identifies the connection; the file descriptor is only the process's local handle.

**Inbound:** a server binds a *LISTEN* socket (the parent) to `:443`. Each completed handshake produces a *child* socket with its own 4-tuple and queues; clients share the server's IP:port but not a connection. Limits: the **accept queue** (finished handshakes waiting for `accept()`), the process's **file-descriptor limit**, and **memory** per socket.

**Outbound:** each connection needs a unique 4-tuple, so one source IP talking to one destination IP:port is limited by its roughly **60,000 ephemeral ports**, and closed connections linger in TIME_WAIT. Many short connections to the same upstream therefore exhaust ports. Fixes: [connection pooling](#/sd/f/connection-pooling) and [multiplexing](#/sd/f/multiplexing) (HTTP/2, gRPC) to reuse a few long-lived connections.

drills.q: A core router between client A and server B reboots and drops traffic for two seconds. A and B had an established TCP connection. What most likely happens?
options: The connection is reset immediately because the pipe broke
The connection survives: lost packets are retransmitted by the endpoints, which hold the connection state
The router restores the connection state from its table
The connection moves to a different path automatically with no loss
drills.explain: Intermediate routers keep no per-connection state. Only the endpoints do, so after the outage unacknowledged segments are retransmitted. (A stateful middlebox such as a NAT or firewall that loses its table would be a different story.)

drills.q: Order the server-side steps of accepting a new client on port 443.
items: Client sends SYN to the LISTEN socket on :443
The kernel completes the three-way handshake and creates a child socket
The established connection waits in the accept queue
The application calls accept() and receives a new file descriptor
The application reads bytes from the child socket's receive queue
drills.explain: The kernel, not the application, completes the handshake. The application only sees the connection when it calls accept(), which is why a slow accept loop fills the queue even though clients have already finished handshaking.

drills.q: A server on :443 has 200,000 clients connected. Someone worries that it "only has 65,535 ports". What is the correct view?
options: They are right; the server cannot exceed about 64k connections
Server-side connections are distinguished by the full 4-tuple, so the real limits are file descriptors, memory and the accept queue
Connections share one socket, so no limit applies
The limit applies only to TLS connections
drills.explain: All of those connections share the server's single port, but each has a different client IP:port, hence a different 4-tuple. The 65k limit bites clients making many connections to a single destination, not servers.

drills.q: A gateway on a single source IP opens a new TCP connection to one upstream IP:port for every request and closes it right after, with no reuse. Assume 60,000 usable ephemeral ports, a TIME_WAIT of 60 s on the closing side (the gateway), and no tcp_tw_reuse. What is the maximum sustained rate of new connections per second to that upstream?
drills.explain: Every closed connection holds its port for 60 s, so each port can serve one connection per minute: 60,000 ports ÷ 60 s = 1,000 connections/s. Beyond that you get 'cannot assign requested address'. Pooling keeps a few connections open and removes the churn entirely.

drills.q: Which fixes reduce ephemeral-port exhaustion on a service that calls the same upstream at high rate? Select all that apply.
options: Keep a pool of persistent connections and reuse them
Use HTTP/2 or gRPC so many requests share one connection
Increase the server-side accept queue on the upstream
Close each connection immediately after its response
drills.explain: Both options reduce the number of distinct 4-tuples consumed. A larger accept queue helps a different limit; closing immediately is exactly what drives TIME_WAIT buildup.
